title: The sword that cuts doubt
hookLine: the Gita praises asking questions and warns against doubt in the same breath
carry: bow, ask, serve, then cut the doubt

lines: TWO IN THE MORNING. STILL DECIDING.
A SWORD, AND ONE CLEAN CUT.
cards: It's two in the morning, and you're still deciding. Take the job or don't. Send the text or don't.
You've made a list of pros and cons, then another list. Every choice looks wrong from some angle. You're not really thinking anymore; you're circling.
That's the Arjuna we met on day one of the Gita, bow on the ground, unable to move. Now Krishna closes chapter four with a picture: a sword, and one clean cut.
The twist: in the very same passage, he tells Arjuna to ask questions. So which is it?

teach.b: Verse thirty-four gives the method for learning. Go to those who have seen the truth, Krishna says. Learn by bowing, by questioning and by serving, and they will teach you.
Three Sanskrit words: pranipata, the bow; pariprashna, asking all around a thing; seva, service. Asking is built right into the path.
Arjuna himself asks question after question for eighteen chapters, and Krishna never scolds him for it. Then the promises.
Even if you were the worst of wrongdoers, verse thirty-six says, you would cross over it all on the raft of knowledge.
And verse thirty-seven: as a blazing fire turns firewood to ash, the fire of knowledge turns all karma to ash.

Then the warning, verse forty: the one without faith, always doubting, is lost; for the doubting self there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness. So what's the difference between a question and a doubt?
A question moves. It wants an answer and will act on one. The doubt Krishna warns about circles forever and keeps you from ever standing up.
Its Sanskrit name, samshaya, is the doubt of a mind hung between two sides, never landing on either.
So the last verse of chapter four: cut this doubt in your heart, born of not knowing, with the sword of knowledge. Take refuge in yoga. Stand up, Arjuna.

teach.h: KEEP THE QUESTIONS. CUT THE CIRCLING.
teach.b: Keep the questions. Cut the circling.

how: Many Hindus learn the Gita from a teacher in the spirit of verse 4.34, with respect, questions and service, and the closing call of chapter four, to cut doubt and stand up, is often cited when facing hard decisions.

o: losing faith in God for good
a question asked to a teacher
doubt that hangs between two sides

games.q: what's inside the verses — tap the pairs.

s: the Gita tells Arjuna to stop asking questions
verse 34 builds questioning into learning, and Arjuna asks for eighteen chapters.
chapter four ends with an image of a sword
verse 42: cut this doubt in your heart with the sword of knowledge, and stand up.
the fire of knowledge only burns bad karma
verse 37 says it turns all karma to ash, as a fire burns firewood.

games.q: you want to learn from someone who has seen the truth. how does verse 34 say to go about it?
o: read alone and trust no one.
wait until all your doubts are gone.
games.why: bow, question, serve. the Gita puts questioning right inside the method, between respect and service.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing you've been circling, not the biggest decision of your life, and ask yourself one real question about it, the kind that has an answer.
On an out-breath, picture the circling as a thread, and let it be cut. You don't have to decide right now; just notice the difference between the question and the loop.

wordCard.voice: Samshaya. Doubt, the mind hung between two sides, never landing on either. Krishna's last words in chapter four: keep asking real questions, but cut the endless circling with the sword of knowledge, and stand up.

orig.note: Sanskrit: samshaya, doubt; the word Krishna uses for the doubt he tells Arjuna to cut.

carryVoice: Your line: bow, ask, serve, then cut the doubt. Questions are part of the path. Chapter four, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.36–4.37 (the raft; knowledge burns karma)
